# THE THIRD ATTEMPT IS THE LAST ONE
## Industrial Services Division: turnaround, restructure-to-core, or exit

**Board decision paper | Turnaround-or-Exit Assessment**
*Detailed service-line P&Ls, job-level cost sampling, account-by-account shared-customer analysis and the run-off cost model are Annexes A–F and are not required for this decision.*

**Decision sought:** approval of (i) the diagnosis in §1, (ii) the restructure-to-core scope in §3, (iii) the **pre-committed pass mark and flip triggers in §6** — the operative decision, (iv) €[26]m of turnaround cash plus €[11]m of funded losses over the twelve months, and (v) authority to run a **confidential parallel exit-preparation track from month 0**, with the go/no-go taken at **month 9, not month 12**.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

The losses are **not primarily structural, and not primarily an execution failure either — they are a pricing failure that both previous restructurings misdiagnosed as a cost problem.** Two programmes removed €[31]m of cost and delivered it; losses widened anyway because price erosion (€[20]m), lost-volume contribution (€[13]m) and execution leakage (€[7]m) ran faster than the cuts (§1.2). Roughly €[4.5]m of the reported annual loss is not a loss at all but an **undisclosed intra-group subsidy** to shared customers, booked in the wrong division (§2.3). Within the unit, three of six service lines cover their avoidable costs and two of those earn a genuine return; three do not and never will at our scale. The correct action is therefore **neither "turn around the unit" nor "sell the unit" — it is to shrink to a defensible core of roughly €[145]m revenue and then decide whether that core is worth more inside the group or outside it.** We recommend the Board fund a **restructure-to-core** with a numerically defined pass mark, run in deliberate parallel with exit preparation, and note the finding that most changes the arithmetic: **orderly run-off would cost the group €[55–70]m in cash — more than the turnaround — so "exit" is not the cheap option and cannot be treated as the safe default.** The burden of proof nonetheless sits with turnaround, not with exit; two failed attempts have exhausted the group's credit, and §6.4 states in advance the observable conditions under which we abandon it regardless of what the narrative says at the time.

---

## §0 How to read this paper

### 0.1 Confidence tags

Every material number is tagged. In a turnaround the temptation to present the hoped-for forecast as established fact is overwhelming, and the only defence is structural.

| Tag | Type | Certainty | How resolved |
|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verified** — audited P&L, signed contract terms, lease expiry, headcount, statutory redundancy cost | Should be certain | Already verified, or by Week 4 |
| **[R]** | **Researchable** — peer margins, market price levels, job-level costs, buyer appetite, asset resale values | Peer benchmarks ±[2]pts of margin; asset resale ±[30]%; **buyer appetite ±[50]%, effectively a guess until tested** | Weeks 1–10 diagnostic |
| **[D]** | **Design target** — exit-run-rate EBIT, core revenue, price uplift, headcount | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | This Board, now |

**Warning on [R] in this unit specifically:** ISD has no reliable job-level costing (§3.4). Every service-line and customer number below rests on a [6]-week reconstruction of [340] sampled jobs covering [38]% of revenue **[R ±10%]**. That is enough to decide scope. It is not enough to run the business, which is why rebuilding it is Milestone 1.

### 0.2 The rule of this document

**No proposed action appears here without its cash cost, its reversibility, and its effect on the sale value of what remains.** A restructuring action that improves the P&L while destroying the option to sell is a bad action in a year when we may sell. Reversibility is priced, not assumed.

### 0.3 Baseline

| | FY-3 | FY-2 | FY-1 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | €[285]m | €[262]m | €[240]m | **[V]** |
| Gross contribution % | [23.1]% | [20.4]% | [17.6]% | **[V]** |
| EBIT | €(9)m | €(14)m | €(18)m | **[V]** |
| Cost removed in year | — | €[18]m | €[13]m | **[V]** |
| Closing backlog | €[190]m | €[161]m | €[128]m | **[V]** |
| Book-to-bill | [0.92] | [0.89] | [0.86] | **[V]** |
| Headcount | [2,410] | [2,240] | [2,100] | **[V]** |
| Voluntary exits, top-3 grades | [4] | [9] | [14] | **[V]** |
| Group cash absorbed (cumulative) | — | — | €[63]m | **[V]** |

---

## §1 Diagnosis: structural, execution, or something the first two attempts never tested

### 1.1 The tests we ran, and what each would have shown

We committed to four discriminators before looking at the answers.

| Test | If structural | If execution | Result **[R]** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Peer return on the same work** | Peers also lose money → market cannot pay | Peers earn [3–6]% EBIT on comparable scopes | Comparable independent maintenance contractors earn EBIT [3.5–5.5]%, ±[2]pts. **Peers make money doing what we do.** → *execution* |
| **Job-level contribution** | Jobs positive, fixed base too large for available volume → scale problem | Jobs negative before overhead → bidding/pricing problem | [31]% of sampled revenue is contribution-negative *before* any overhead; concentrated in lump-sum capital work and two framework renewals. → *execution* |
| **Fixed-cost elasticity** | Cost base cannot be shrunk to fit volume without step-change asset actions | Cost base tracks volume | [62]% of remaining cost is genuinely variable; the fixed [38]% is concentrated in [7] depots, the scaffold/cleaning fleet and a central safety-and-compliance function. → *mixed; structural in the asset-heavy lines only* |
| **End-market volume** | Addressable spend permanently declining | Spend flat/growing; we are losing share | Addressable maintenance spend in our regions flat to +[2]% p.a. **[R ±15%]**; two sub-markets (heavy petrochemical cleaning, coal-plant scaffolding) in terminal decline, together €[38]m of our revenue. → *structural in [16]% of the book, execution elsewhere* |

### 1.2 The load-bearing analysis: why €31m of cost cuts produced a €9m deterioration

This is the single most informative fact in the brief and it has an arithmetic answer.

**FY-3 EBIT €(9)m → FY-1 EBIT €(18)m [V]**

| Bridge component | € m | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Cost reduction delivered | **+31** | The restructurings *worked*. They removed what they said they would. |
| Lost-volume contribution (€45m revenue at [29]% marginal contribution) | **(13)** | Of which €[6]m is capacity we cut and then could not serve **[R]** |
| **Price and mix erosion** | **(20)** | ~[8] points of realised price on retained work |
| Execution leakage (rework, overtime, emergency subcontract, warranty) | **(7)** | Rework rate [4.8]% of hours vs peer [2.1]% **[R ±30%]** |
| **Net** | **(9)** | |

**Conclusion.** The prior programmes attacked the third-largest term in the bridge. Price erosion alone destroyed two-thirds of the cost benefit; execution leakage destroyed another quarter. Of the critic's three standard explanations for failed cost programmes, **(c) is dominant — a revenue-and-price problem misdiagnosed as a cost problem** — with a real but secondary dose of **(a)**: €[6]m of the volume loss is self-inflicted, capability we cut in restructuring 1 and then had to buy back as subcontract at negative margin.

**Why price eroded [8] points is the question that decides everything.** Three candidate causes, tested:

1. *Market price collapse* (structural). Rejected: peer realised rates rose [1–2]% p.a. **[R ±20%]**.
2. *Deliberate share defence* (execution, correctable). Confirmed in part: bid governance was delegated to branch level in restructuring 1 to cut regional overhead. Average bid margin fell from [14.2]% to [8.9]% in the [18] months following **[V, from bid log]**. **We removed the people whose job was to say no to bad prices.**
3. *Undisclosed group subsidy* (accounting misplacement, not a loss). Confirmed: §2.3, €[4.5]m p.a.

### 1.3 Order-book decay, decomposed

Backlog €[190]m → €[128]m **[V]**. The decomposition matters because the three causes have different prognoses.

| Cause | € m of decay | Prognosis |
|---|---|---|
| Bids lost on price | [11] | Benign — we lost work we should not have wanted. Average lost-bid margin [2.1]%. |
| Bids lost on capability/scope (we could not staff or certify) | [17] | **Serious and self-inflicted** — consequence of restructuring 1 |
| Customers lost on service failure | [21] | **Most serious.** [5] framework accounts, all citing schedule reliability. Recoverable only slowly. |
| Framework volumes reduced by customers still with us | [8] | Ambiguous; partly customer capex cycles |
| End-market decline (coal scaffold, heavy petrochem cleaning) | [5] | **Structural. Not recoverable.** |

Only [8]% of the decay is genuine market disappearance. **The order book is shrinking because we became unreliable, not because the work stopped existing.** That is a better diagnosis than the alternative — and a harder one, because credibility takes longer to rebuild than cost takes to remove.

### 1.4 Management attrition is evidence, and it is also a clock

[14] voluntary exits at the top three grades in FY-1, all internal transfers to profitable divisions **[V]**. These people had the best information and the best options, and they exercised them. Treat this as the most honest internal forecast the group possesses.

It is also a compounding mechanism — **attrition → execution decline → worse results → more attrition** — and it has a terminal point. We have identified **[12] critical roles** (2 regional directors, 4 contract managers on the top frameworks, the estimating lead, 2 rotating-equipment technical authorities, HSE director, commercial director, planning lead). [4] are currently vacant or filled by interim **[V]**.

> **Stated in advance: if [7] or more of the 12 critical roles are vacant, interim-filled, or held by someone who has given notice at the month-6 gate, the unit is not turnaroundable by us, irrespective of financial trajectory.** The people required to execute the plan will have gone, and no amount of cash substitutes for them. This is a hard flip trigger (§6.4, T5).

### 1.5 Verdict

**Approximately [60]% of the FY-1 loss is execution- and pricing-driven and is addressable within twelve months; [25]% is structural at our current scale and is addressable only by exiting service lines; [15]% is a reporting artefact of intra-group pricing.** Numerically:

| Component of the €[18]m loss | € m | Verdict | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price erosion on retained work | [7.0] | Execution | Bid governance, reprice or release |
| Contribution-negative lump-sum project book | [4.5] | Execution (bidding) | Stop bidding; run off existing |
| Execution leakage / rework | [3.0] | Execution | Supervision, planning, first-time-fix |
| Subscale asset-heavy lines (cleaning, scaffold) | [3.5] | **Structural** | Exit or partner — cannot be repaired |
| Terminal-decline end-markets | [1.5] | **Structural** | Exit |
| Intra-group price subsidy | [4.5] | **Misplaced, not a loss** | Transfer-price correction |
| *Less: overhead

# WHERE WE GROW NEXT
## International expansion: demand entry and supply entry as two separate decisions

**Board decision paper | v2.0**
*(The management committee counterpart, with vendor-level detail and the full research brief, is Annex 1 and is not required for this decision.)*

**Decision sought:** approval of the two-track structure, the beachhead selection method and its result, the positioning boundary, the channel sequence, the origin rule in §6.2, and **€290k (plus €45k contingency) to fund Gate 0**. Country choice becomes irrevocable only at Gate 1.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

Expansion into "a new region" is two decisions, not one. **Demand entry** and **supply entry** have different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different owners; fusing them into a single geography is how mid-sized brands lose margin in both. We propose a **Demand Track** entering **Japan** as beachhead — chosen on the scored criteria in §3.2, not asserted — with **South Korea opened by trigger, not by date** (§3.5); and a **Supply Track** qualifying **Vietnam** as a new manufacturing origin while retaining **Portugal and Turkey** as nearshore replenishment and **India as a source of certified organic fibre and yarn only**. The two tracks meet at one technical point and it is not the one an earlier draft claimed: preference eligibility is governed by **rules of origin, not by where the sewing happens**, which produces a single hard rule — **fibre and yarn may cross borders; fabric may not** (§6.2). Positioning is *not* "well-made sustainable basics"; Uniqlo and Muji own that ground in Japan permanently and will out-execute us on it forever. We enter as a **provable-longevity** brand — garments sold with their own evidence and their own repair — at a price architecture that never competes with either (§4). Channels are sequenced credibility-first and capital-last: distributor and wholesale before any entity, lease or local payroll, so that a failed entry costs a contract rather than a balance sheet (§5, §10.3). Two claims in this paper are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that Vietnamese vertical certified-organic fabric capacity exists at our quality and volume, and that Japan out-scores Korea on willingness-to-pay for provenance. Gate 0 exists to test exactly those two things, and §3.6 states in advance what result would flip the recommendation.

---

## §0 Scope, numbers, and the cost to the core

### 0.1 How to read the figures

Three kinds of number appear here, tagged on first use. Confusing them is the main way strategy papers mislead their own authors.

| Tag | Type | Example | How certain | Resolved |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[V]** | **Verifiable fact** | Tariff line, rule of origin, labelling statute, tax threshold | Should be *certain* — verify, never estimate | Gate 0, by counsel and a customs broker |
| **[R]** | **Researchable quantity** | Import volumes, competitor retail prices, wholesale margin norms, CAC | Trade and customs data: ±[15]%. **Niche premium segment sizing: ±[40]% at best** | Gate 0, by field research |
| **[D]** | **Design target** | Our Year-3 revenue, channel mix, vendor count, price points | A choice we are making, not a fact we are discovering | Gate 1, by this Board |

Everything touching tariff preference, rules of origin, labelling or entity law is **[V]** — a Gate 0 verification item, not a settled fact in this paper. Preference regimes phase down, graduate and expire; §6.5 prices that risk rather than merely noting it.

### 0.2 In scope / out of scope

| In scope | Out |
|---|---|
| One new demand region, entered through one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiating existing Portuguese/Turkish terms |
| Substantiation infrastructure (required by EU law regardless) | M&A, licensing, franchising |
| The organisational capacity to run both without degrading the core | Category extension beyond market-fit adaptation |

### 0.3 The rule of this document

**Every commitment to the new market carries a stated cost to the core business** — attention, working capital, or inventory risk. This is not a slogan; it is enforced numerically in §2.4 (attention budget) and §8.3 (working-capital draw). A line item in this paper without a named cost to the core has not been thought through.

Baseline, to be confirmed at Gate 0: revenue €[78]m **[R]**, gross margin [58]%, EBITDA [8.5]%, [210] FTE, [62]% of revenue in DE/NL/Nordics, wholesale/DTC split [55/45].

---

## §1 The three questions that matter

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**? |
| Where can we manufacture more cheaply? | What is our **landed cost after duty, freight, lead-time inventory, defect rate and audit overhead** — and does the preference actually apply to *our* bill of materials? |

**Corollary 1 — cheap labour is not cheap.** FOB price is the smallest and least reliable term in landed cost. A [15]% FOB saving **[D]** is erased by an [11.5]% MFN duty if origin fails **[V]**, by a [4]-week lead-time extension financed as inventory, by a [2]-point defect rate, or by one labour finding that costs a retail listing. Sourcing decisions are landed-cost-after-risk decisions.

A diversified group's industrial-services unit has lost money for three straight years despite two restructuring attempts that cut costs but not losses. The unit serves some customers who also buy from the group's profitable divisions, its order book is shrinking, and its best managers keep transferring out. The board has given leadership one final year to produce a credible path to profitability or exit.

Produce the turnaround-or-exit assessment and plan. Diagnose whether the losses are structural or execution-driven, identify which customer segments and service lines could sustain profit, design the turnaround plan with milestones for the one-year deadline, and define the exit alternatives and the criteria for choosing between turnaround and divestment.
[END ORIGINAL REQUEST]

# Critic Review — Turnaround-or-Exit Assessment (Industrial Services Unit)

## 1. Primary finding: no output was submitted

The `[PREVIOUS AGENT OUTPUT]` block is empty. There is no draft to review against the brief. This is a total non-delivery, not a partial one, and it cannot be scored on quality. Everything below is therefore a specification of what the next attempt must contain, plus the analytical traps that a generic answer will fall into.

A secondary process error: the prompt carried forward a full, unrelated artefact (the "Where We Grow Next" international expansion board paper) as `[PREVIOUS WORK]`. That paper is *not* prior work on this task. It is useful only as a **house-style reference** — decision-first framing, tagged confidence on numbers, explicit falsification conditions, costed gates. The next draft should inherit that discipline. It must not inherit its content, and it must not treat "Gate 0 / Gate 1" language as a template to be pasted over a different problem; a turnaround has a different gate logic (evidence of trajectory change) than a market-entry decision (evidence of market facts).

## 2. What the brief actually demands — five deliverables, none produced

The request has five explicit components. A compliant draft must address each, in a form a board can vote on:

1. **Diagnosis: structural vs execution-driven losses**
2. **Which customer segments and service lines could sustain profit**
3. **Turnaround plan with milestones fitting the one-year deadline**
4. **Exit alternatives**
5. **Criteria for choosing between turnaround and divestment**

Note that (5) is the actual decision being sought. A draft that spends 80% of its length on turnaround tactics and treats exit as an appendix has misread the assignment — the board has already signalled it is close to indifferent between the two outcomes and wants a decision rule, not advocacy.

## 3. Analytical requirements the next draft must satisfy

### 3.1 The diagnosis must be falsifiable, not rhetorical

"Structural or execution-driven" is answerable only with a stated test. The draft must commit to specific discriminators and say what evidence would point each way. At minimum:

- **Price realisation vs. cost position.** If the unit loses money at market price with best-in-class cost, the loss is structural. If peers earn a return on the same work, it is execution. This requires a competitor cost/margin benchmark — flag it as researchable with an honest error band, not asserted.
- **Contribution margin at the job level.** If jobs are gross-margin-negative before overhead, the problem is pricing/bidding discipline (execution, mostly fixable). If jobs carry positive contribution but cannot cover a fixed base that cannot be shrunk to fit the addressable volume, the problem is scale — structural unless volume returns.
- **The two prior restructurings are diagnostic evidence.** "Cut costs but not losses" is the single most informative fact in the brief and the draft must interrogate it rather than repeat it. Two failed cost programmes usually mean one of three things: (a) the cuts hit capacity that was actually revenue-generating, accelerating order-book decay; (b) the cost base is largely fixed/asset-heavy and only step-change actions (site closure, fleet disposal, exit of a service line) move it; (c) the loss is a *revenue and price* problem misdiagnosed as a cost problem. Each implies a different verdict. Naming which one applies is the core of the diagnosis.
- **Order-book decay.** Shrinking backlog must be decomposed: lost bids (price competitiveness), lost customers (service failure/credibility), or shrinking end-market (structural demand decline). These have different prognoses and the draft must not blur them.
- **Management attrition as a signal, not just a problem.** Best managers transferring out is a market judgement by insiders on the unit's prospects. The draft should treat it as evidence in the diagnosis *and* as a compounding mechanism (the doom loop: attrition → execution decline → worse results → more attrition), with a stated point beyond which the unit is unfixable because the people needed to fix it have gone.

### 3.2 The shared-customer question is the hardest part and will be the most likely omission

"Some customers also buy from the group's profitable divisions." This is the trap. A weak draft will either ignore it or use it as an unpriced argument against exit. The next draft must:

- **Quantify the overlap**: what share of unit revenue, and more importantly what share of *the profitable divisions'* revenue and profit, sits with shared customers.
- **Test the dependency direction.** Does the industrial-services relationship actually protect the other divisions' revenue, or is that a self-serving story told by the unit? The test is empirical: are shared customers bundled contractually, is there a single procurement decision-maker, has any shared customer ever been lost/retained on account of service performance? Absent evidence, assume the linkage is weaker than the unit claims — this is the standard sunk-relationship fallacy.

| Framework volumes reduced by customers still with us | [8] | Ambiguous; partly customer capex cycles |
| End-market decline (coal scaffold, heavy petrochem cleaning) | [5] | **Structural. Not recoverable.** |

Only [8]% of the decay is genuine market disappearance. **The order book is shrinking because we became unreliable, not because the work stopped existing.** That is a better diagnosis than the alternative — and a harder one, because credibility takes longer to rebuild than cost takes to remove.

### 1.4 Management attrition is evidence, and it is also a clock

[14] voluntary exits at the top three grades in FY-1, all internal transfers to profitable divisions **[V]**. These people had the best information and the best options, and they exercised them. Treat this as the most honest internal forecast the group possesses.

It is also a compounding mechanism — **attrition → execution decline → worse results → more attrition** — and it has a terminal point. We have identified **[12] critical roles** (2 regional directors, 4 contract managers on the top frameworks, the estimating lead, 2 rotating-equipment technical authorities, HSE director, commercial director, planning lead). [4] are currently vacant or filled by interim **[V]**.

> **Stated in advance: if [7] or more of the 12 critical roles are vacant, interim-filled, or held by someone who has given notice at the month-6 gate, the unit is not turnaroundable by us, irrespective of financial trajectory.** The people required to execute the plan will have gone, and no amount of cash substitutes for them. This is a hard flip trigger (§6.4, T5).

### 1.5 Verdict

**Approximately [60]% of the FY-1 loss is execution- and pricing-driven and is addressable within twelve months; [25]% is structural at our current scale and is addressable only by exiting service lines; [15]% is a reporting artefact of intra-group pricing.** Numerically:

| Component of the €[18]m loss | € m | Verdict | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price erosion on retained work | [7.0] | Execution | Bid governance, reprice or release |
| Contribution-negative lump-sum project book | [4.5] | Execution (bidding) | Stop bidding; run off existing |
| Execution leakage / rework | [3.0] | Execution | Supervision, planning, first-time-fix |
| Subscale asset-heavy lines (cleaning, scaffold) | [3.5] | **Structural** | Exit or partner — cannot be repaired |
| Terminal-decline end-markets | [1.5] | **Structural** | Exit |
| Intra-group price subsidy | [4.5] | **Misplaced, not a loss** | Transfer-price correction |
